question:
A 57-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of fever, headache, otalgia, nasal congestion, and hearing loss. Laboratory workup reveals anti-proteinase 3 antibody positivity (PR3 664.3) and cytoplasmic ANCA at a titer of 1:10. Renal function, antinuclear antibody profile, T-SPOT, and fungal studies are all within normal limits. He is treated with methylprednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and antibiotics, with resolution of fever, otalgia, and hearing loss. Over the following year, he develops recurrent headaches and new-onset lumbodorsal pain. Enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates an abnormal signal in the epidural space at the posterior margin of T10–T12. Surgical resection of the lesion is performed. Histopathology of the resected tissue shows necrotic tissue, fibrous tissue, and granulation tissue hyperplasia with calcification, extensive acute and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration, and focal epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells. Special stains for fungi (GMS, PAS) and acid-fast bacilli are all negative. Subsequently, enhanced brain MRI reveals significant dural thickening in the bilateral cerebellar, posterior cranial fossa, and foramen magnum regions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated mononuclear cells (35 × 10⁶/L), nucleated cells (40 × 10⁶/L), and protein (1.49 g/L), with negative cultures.

question:
A 52-year-old male with a long-standing smoking history and chronic bronchitis presents with a 2-week history of weakness and anorexia followed by one week of fever unresponsive to antibiotics. He develops blood-stained sputum, epistaxis, and bilateral eye congestion; an ophthalmologist diagnoses scleritis. Chest CT shows extensive consolidation in the right lower lobe with pleural effusion. Laboratory findings include CRP 358 mg/L, WBC 13,020/μL, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, platelets 623,000/μL, proteinuria (1+), urine RBC 205/μL, urine WBC 60/μL with 1–2 WBC casts per high-power field, 24-hour urine protein 1512 mg/day, serum creatinine 65 µmol/L, and serum albumin 29 g/L. ANCA testing reveals cANCA titer 1:40 and PR3-ANCA 988.8 CU. CT-guided lung biopsy demonstrates multiple granulomas, multinucleated giant cell hyperplasia, inflammatory cell infiltration, and focal necrosis in the blood vessel wall. Four days after starting methylprednisolone 80 mg/day, he develops sudden right abdominal pain with intermittent hematuria; hemoglobin drops to 6.8 g/dL and serum creatinine rises to 103 µmol/L. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirms a subcapsular hemorrhage of the right kidney.

question:

He has been receiving sintilimab (anti-PD-1) for 16 months, along with one cycle of paclitaxel and carboplatin. He has a 10-year history of hypertension and no prior history of drug-induced photosensitivity. question:
A 5-year-old male born at 37 weeks to non-consanguineous parents of European and European/Native American descent presents with microcephaly (head circumference z-score −2.83 at birth), low birth weight, global developmental delay, hypotonia, failure to thrive, short stature, and feeding difficulties requiring G-tube placement. Examination reveals dry, cracked, itchy skin lesions on the face and trunk, and hair shaft analysis under polarized light microscopy demonstrates alternating dark and light bands. Serial brain MRIs over 4.5 years show progressive diffuse T2 hyperintensity in supratentorial white matter with poor gray-white differentiation on T1-weighted images, consistent with progressive hypomyelination. He has photosensitivity but no increased freckling or elevated skin cancer risk. An Autism/ID gene panel identifies compound heterozygous variants in a gene encoding a subunit of the TFIIH transcription/DNA repair complex: a paternal splice junction loss (c.2190+1delG) and a maternal pathogenic variant (c.1479+2dupT). Methylation analysis for Prader-Willi syndrome and a 180-gene epilepsy panel are both normal.

A 37-year-old Kuwaiti woman presents with a 3-day history of occipital headache and left arm paresthesia. She had a prior lacunar ischemic stroke 2 months earlier with no residual deficits and was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy. She reports a 5-year history of recurrent oral and genital ulcers and a 2-year history of intermittent left knee pain and swelling. She takes oral contraceptives but does not smoke and has no traditional cerebrovascular risk factors. On examination she is afebrile with normal vital signs; neurological testing reveals left-sided hypoesthesia with intact motor power, and she has active oral ulcerations. Bilateral ankle tenderness and swelling are noted. A pathergy test is negative. Brain MRI shows a small area of restricted diffusion in the anterior right thalamus consistent with a recent lacunar infarct, patchy high T2/FLAIR signal in the right thalamus extending to the cerebral peduncle, bilateral basal ganglia, and left putamen compatible with vasculitis, and old lacunar foci in the right periventricular and subcortical frontal regions; MRA shows no stenotic lesions. Cardiac workup including echocardiography and 24-hour ECG is normal. Carotid Doppler is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show mild normocytic normochromic anemia, ESR 81 mm/hour, CRP 40.8 mg/dL, and HLA-B51 positivity. Antiphospholipid antibodies, antinuclear antibody, ANCA, factor V Leiden, proteins C and S, antithrombin III, homocysteine, lipid profile, glucose, and infectious serologies are all within normal limits.

question:
A man is first evaluated in his 20s for recurrent primary pneumothorax. He has increased skin laxity most prominent at the neck, thigh, and forearm, a history of easy bruising with thigh and forearm haematomas after contact sports, mildly increased range of motion of joints, atrophic scarring, and moderate pectus excavatum. There are no spine deformities, no Marfanoid ectasia, and no family history of connective tissue disorders. Molecular testing later reveals a COL5A2 mutation in exon 29 (c.1977 G>A). Evaluation for Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and EDS type IV is negative. Over subsequent decades he develops spontaneous haemothorax, Stanford B aortic dissection in the absence of pre-existing hypertension or aortic aneurysm, and ultimately fatal mesenteric haemorrhage.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_options: {"A": "Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV)", "B": "Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome", "C": "Marfan syndrome", "D": "Loeys-Dietz syndrome", "E": "Hypermobility Ehlers-Danlos syndrome"}

question:
A 26-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a painless lump in the right breast that became painful 3 days prior. Physical examination shows no skin erythema, nipple discharge, or features of neurofibromatosis (no café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, or cutaneous neurofibromas). Laboratory results are normal. Ultrasonography reveals a 0.86 × 0.64 cm oval hypoechoic nodule with clear boundaries and uniform internal echogenicity located 0.41 cm beneath the skin in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast; color Doppler imaging shows no significant internal blood flow. Histopathology demonstrates an encapsulated tumor with alternating densely cellular (Antoni A) and loosely cellular (Antoni B) areas; the Antoni A areas contain spindle cells arranged in palisading and swirling patterns with characteristic structures composed of two parallel rows of tightly arranged nuclei separated by eosinophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry shows strong diffuse positivity for S-100 and SOX10, a Ki-67 index of less than 2%, and negativity for CKpan, P63, CK5/6, C-erbB-2, CD117, DOG-1, SMA, desmin, and synaptophysin.

question:

She subsequently received anastrozole with no evidence of recurrence. Four years after completing radiotherapy, she developed erythematous and violaceous skin changes on the left breast that progressed over 3 months to a cardboard-like texture with pruritus and severe bilateral breast deformities. Lesions began in the left inframammary region, then extended to the right breast, abdominal folds, and along the spine. New lesions appeared at sites of skin friction (Koebner phenomenon). She has no symptoms of connective tissue disease and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Breast ultrasound shows diffuse skin thickening extending into the adipose tissue without suspicious underlying lesions. Mammogram, breast MRI, and physical examination show no evidence of cancer recurrence. Skin biopsy demonstrates dermal fibrosclerosis, chronic inflammatory remodeling, epidermal atrophy, and endothelial and fibroblastic remodeling.

She has no constitutional symptoms. Immunohistochemistry shows the atypical lymphocytes are CD3+, CD4+ (predominant, CD4:CD8 ratio >4:1), with approximately 50% reduction in CD7 expression relative to CD3, and approximately 20% CD30 positivity. Follicular helper T-cell markers (BCL6, CD10, PD1, TOX) are negative or minimally positive. EBER staining is negative. Whole-body PET scan and peripheral blood flow cytometry show no systemic involvement. Following discontinuation of methotrexate, the cutaneous lesions largely regress.

His medical history is significant for HIV-1 infection with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 405 cells/μL, as well as chronic parvovirus B19 infection. Complete blood count reveals neutrophilia (85.1%) without leukocytosis, and inflammatory markers are elevated (ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 8.99 mg/dL). Skin biopsy demonstrates a normal epidermis with neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate, both interstitial and perivascular, in the superficial dermis, along with capillary ectasia in the papillary dermis and no evidence of vasculitis. He undergoes extended parotidectomy; histopathology shows nests of malignant epithelial cells surrounded by massive lymphocytic infiltration, immunohistochemistry positive for CK5/6 and p63 with Ki-67 of 60%, and in situ hybridization positive for EBER. A 7-year-old girl is referred after excision of a 5 mm nodular lesion on her right upper leg. Six months prior, a 1 mm reddish-gray skin change was noted; one month before excision it had nearly tripled in volume and changed to a brownish hue with a central grayish area. She has no complaints, and family history is negative for atypical moles or malignancies. Histopathology of the excised specimen shows large epithelioid melanocytes with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and abundant pigmented cytoplasm, predominantly within the dermis with some epidermal involvement, coalescing nests and sheets, pleomorphic nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and deep dermal tumor cells lacking maturation surrounded by a lymphocytic infiltrate. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates a medium-to-high Ki-67 proliferation index extending to the base of the lesion and diffuse loss of p16 expression. Breslow depth is 1.77 mm, Clark level III, with vertical growth phase and mitotic activity but no lymphatic invasion.

A 56-year-old man with no prior medical history presents to the ICU with a 20-day history of pharyngeal pain, progressive dysphagia, diffuse myalgia, oliguria, and cola-colored urine. He had engaged in heavy manual labor approximately 3–4 weeks before symptom onset. On examination he has severe pharyngolaryngeal edema, generalized muscle tenderness, and bilateral upper-extremity edema. Laboratory studies reveal ALT 246 U/L, AST 818 U/L, LDH 1,775 U/L, CK 11,064 U/L, serum myoglobin >1,000 ng/mL, IL-6 33.99 pg/mL, and CRP 39.03 mg/L. A 15-item male tumor marker panel is unremarkable. Chest CT shows bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Despite aggressive intravenous hydration, urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate, and continuous renal-replacement therapy, CK levels continue to rise after CRRT is paused and he develops rapidly progressive proximal limb weakness—he can no longer lift his arms above the horizontal. Electromyography demonstrates abundant spontaneous activity in proximal muscles and short-duration, low-amplitude motor-unit potentials consistent with a myopathic pattern. Non-contrast MRI of both lower legs shows diffuse intramuscular and subcutaneous edema with patchy T1 and T2 hyperintensity and prominent tortuous vascular signal. Cervical MRI reveals marked swelling of the posterior cervical musculature and pre-vertebral fascia. Myositis-specific antibody profiling returns positive for anti-NXP-2 at a titer of 1:100. Open biopsy of the left deltoid discloses endomysial and perimysial infiltrates composed of CD3+ T cells and CD38+ plasma cells, with focal sarcolemmal deposition of PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive, Congo red–negative material.

question:
A 55-year-old male with a history of hypertension and smoking presents with persistent chest pain for 13 hours. ECG shows Q-wave formation, T-wave inversion in leads II, III, and aVF, and right bundle branch block. Cardiac biomarkers including cTnI, CK-MB, and myoglobin are elevated. Coronary angiography reveals subtotal occlusion of the mid right coronary artery and diffuse stenosis of the proximal-to-mid left anterior descending artery. He undergoes PCI with stent implantation and is discharged. One month later he is readmitted for residual vasculopathy; cTnI, CK-MB, and myoglobin remain persistently elevated despite successful revascularization. On careful re-inquiry, the patient reports skin tightness in the extremities, exertional dyspnea, and fingertip pain in cold weather. Physical examination reveals dark, stiff skin on both forearms. Serum ANA is positive; ACA and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are negative. Creatine kinase is significantly elevated. Chest CT shows pulmonary fibrosis in the lower lobes. Cardiac MRI demonstrates late gadolinium enhancement in the inferior wall subendocardial myocardium and diffuse myocardial fibrosis on T1 mapping with elevated extracellular volume. Skin biopsy reveals dermal and subcutaneous thickening with fibrous tissue hyperplasia, reduced cutaneous appendages, and focal chronic inflammation.

question:

Fourteen days after starting a new oral androgen-receptor antagonist, he developed a rash on the abdomen and upper limbs that spread to involve the entire body with pruritus. Despite discontinuation of the medication and treatment with a topical corticosteroid, symptoms progressed. Two months later he developed whole-body skin exudation and large-scale desquamation accompanied by low-grade fever. On admission, temperature is 39.0°C. question:

His mother reports that he developed skin lesions over his face, neck, and extremities beginning at age 1 year and 9 months. His 2-year-old younger brother has similar skin lesions. Physical examination reveals a fungating, erythematous, ulcerated mass arising from the right medial palpebral conjunctiva. Dermatologic examination demonstrates atrophic, dry, scaly skin with alternating hyperpigmented and hypopigmented patches and lentigos over his face, neck, hands, and legs. Histopathologic examination of an incisional biopsy of the conjunctival mass shows full-thickness dysplastic squamous epithelium, cords of pleomorphic round-to-polygonal cells with a desmoplastic stromal response, keratin pearl formation, and brisk mitotic activity. CT scan of the orbit reveals intraocular invasion and orbital soft tissue involvement without bone or brain invasion.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis explaining this child's constellation of cutaneous, ocular, and familial findings?
answer_options: {"A": "Xeroderma pigmentosum", "B": "Oculocutaneous albinism", "C": "Rothmund-Thomson syndrome", "D": "Cockayne syndrome", "E": "Dyskeratosis congenita"}

question:
A 33-year-old Caucasian woman presents with skin fragility limited to the limbs since infancy, with onset of blistering within two months of birth. Examination reveals thin scars, fragile clear fluid-filled blisters, and well-demarcated erosions with bright pink bases containing serous, hemorrhagic, and purulent exudate. She reports intermittent severe pruritus. Mucous membranes are uninvolved. Fingernails and toenails are partially preserved but dystrophic, thickened, and yellowish. Both parents were clinically unaffected. Whole-exome sequencing identifies a homozygous nonsense variant in the LAMB3 gene (p.Gln834Ter), resulting in a premature termination codon in the β3 subunit of laminin 5. Immunohistochemical staining of a skin biopsy shows only focal, non-specific positivity for laminin β3 in the basement membrane zone.

A 31-year-old woman presents with several months of recurrent nasal crusting and episodes of epistaxis, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and arthralgia affecting the small joints of her hands. Laboratory tests show normal inflammatory markers but reveal eosinophilia on full blood count. Chest imaging is unremarkable. A nasal biopsy demonstrates moderately severe inflammation. Serological testing reveals an elevated PR3-ANCA level of 12 IU/mL (normal < 3.5 IU/mL). She is started on methotrexate, later switched to azathioprine, and ultimately escalated to rituximab, yet continues to experience nasal crusting, recurrent epistaxis, and worsening joint pain. Examination reveals a mass larger than 6 cm in the upper outer quadrant and a smaller mass in the lower outer quadrant, both with imprecise borders, without skin erythema, nipple retraction, or breast tenderness. Ultrasound reveals hypoechoic, irregular masses with spiculated margins. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy is performed. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of ectatic vessels lined by endothelial cells without atypia, a fibroelastic stroma, and aggregation of hemosiderophages. A 29-year-old woman presents with a two-year history of recurrent oral ulcers, a one-year history of genital ulcers, and persistent thrombocytopenia. She was previously admitted for acute small bowel perforation requiring segmental resection of the ileum, ileocecal region, and ascending colon. Karyotype analysis demonstrates trisomy 8 and trisomy 9. She is classified as IPSS intermediate-2 and IPSS-R high-risk. She subsequently develops recurrent anastomotic and descending colon ulcers despite escalating doses of a TNF-α inhibitor.

She was initially misdiagnosed with cyclic vomiting syndrome. At age 5, she developed swelling of the genital and perineal regions after minor bicycle-related trauma. Subsequently, she experienced multiple episodes of peripheral swelling involving the hands, feet, and lips, often triggered by minor trauma. Episodes were unresponsive to antihistamines and corticosteroids but resolved spontaneously within 2–3 days. Some attacks were preceded by erythema marginatum. Laboratory evaluation reveals low C4, low C1-inhibitor antigenic levels, and markedly low C1-inhibitor functional activity. Neither parent has a history of angioedema, and both parents have normal C4 and normal C1-inhibitor levels and function. Nasal endoscopy reveals a midline granulomatous lesion. CT chest shows right mid-zone consolidation with bilateral pulmonary nodules; CT temporal bone shows otomastoiditis. Laboratory studies reveal ESR 90 mm/hr, CRP 165 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.44 ng/mL, normal complement levels, and normal urinalysis. Immunofluorescence shows positive c-ANCA; ELISA shows strongly positive anti-PR3 (95.01 U/mL) with negative anti-MPO and p-ANCA. Skin biopsy shows vasculitic features without immune complex deposition. ANA and ACE are negative. Cultures for acid-fast bacilli are negative, and hepatitis B, C, and HIV screens are negative.

By day 3, he develops melena. CT angiography of the abdomen shows no mesenteric ischemia but reveals 7.1 mm thickening of the second duodenal segment. Gastroscopy demonstrates edematous, friable mucosa with scalloping and multiple 3–5 mm clean-based ulcers in the second and third duodenal segments with mild spontaneous oozing. Capsule endoscopy reveals more than 20 small intestinal ulcerations. Urgent enteroscopy shows multiple duodenal (D3–D4) and jejunal ulcers up to 2 cm × 2 cm. Biopsy of the ulcers shows duodenal mucosa with maintained villous architecture, no neutrophilic activity, no evidence of small vessel vasculitis, but a single intranuclear inclusion body with a surrounding halo in an endothelial cell. Chest high-resolution CT demonstrates interlobular septal thickening and subpleural ground-glass opacities. Laboratory evaluation reveals a markedly elevated serum titer of an autoantibody associated with innate antiviral RNA sensing (titer 328.76; normal range 200–250) and a positive antinuclear antibody at 1:80. Serum ferritin and KL-6 are elevated, and peripheral blood lymphocyte count is decreased. Despite high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, cyclophosphamide, and tacrolimus, her respiratory status worsens and she requires invasive mechanical ventilation. A 6-month-old male infant presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of unexplained persistent fever and mild cough. Initial workup shows leukocytosis (WBC 16.6 × 10⁹/L with 73.1% neutrophils) and elevated CRP (42.1 mg/L) and ESR (54 mm/h). He is treated with ceftriaxone for 2 days without improvement. On the 6th day of illness, he develops a generalized congestive rash, bilateral conjunctival congestion without exudate, flushed and chapped lips, limb swelling, right cervical lymphadenopathy, and erythema at the BCG vaccination site. Repeat labs show WBC 15.4 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 106 g/L, platelets 430 × 10⁹/L, CRP 55.5 mg/L, ALT 280 U/L, and AST 231 U/L. Cardiac injury markers (cTnI, CK-MB, myoglobin) are within normal limits. Echocardiography reveals a small aneurysm of the left coronary artery (Z-score 3.27) and dilation of the left anterior descending artery (Z-score 2.01). Upon admission, cardiac auscultation reveals a heart rate of 190 bpm with regular rhythm. The infant is afebrile at 38°C, quiet at rest, with normal blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and urine output. ECG shows a ventricular rate of 219 bpm, regular rhythm, normal QRS morphology, and retrograde P' waves in leads aVR and II with an RP interval of 93 ms (RP < PR). Two COVID-19 nucleic acid tests are negative.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis explaining this infant's cardiac rhythm abnormality?

A 41-year-old woman presents with a solitary, slowly enlarging mass on her left lower flank that she first noticed 10 years ago. She reports cyclic pain associated with her menstrual cycle. Physical examination reveals a 7.5 × 6 cm skin-colored, immobile nodule with an elevated center; no ulceration, café-au-lait macules, or hypertrichosis are noted. CT scan demonstrates a 5.7 × 8.4 × 5.8 cm fatty mass in the subcutaneous layer, initially suggesting a benign lipoma. Surgical excision is performed, and histopathological examination of the 8.7 × 6.0 × 6.0 cm yellowish, soft, lobulated, encapsulated specimen reveals an aggregation of mature adipocytes throughout the reticular dermis, embedded among collagen bundles and constituting more than 50% of the dermis. No glandular tissue is identified on microscopy.
